resolutions.researcher_notes: OPEC ASB 2012 (live, still hosted at opec.org, 200) Table 4.10 'Gas pipelines in OPEC Members, 2011', p.75, lists 'Attahaddy/km-91.5' operated by Sirte Oil as an active catalogued asset (pdftotext-confirmed manually at the exact page the seed citation names; the automated substring screen FAILs on 'Attahaddy'/'Sirte Oil' only because the verifier's PDF-text extraction doesn't reach page ~75 of this large document -- a content-depth false negative, not a dead link; liveness (200) and the literal text were both hand-confirmed via `pdftotext -layout`). Independently, a Libya Observer article dated 15 Mar 2026 reports NOC pumping gas through 'the connection point at kilometer 91 within the pipeline network of the Sirte Oil and Gas Production and Manufacturing Company' toward Brega -- confirming that junction/network segment is presently live, 15 years after the OPEC snapshot. Status is inferred from context in both (neither uses the literal word 'operating'), per protocol guidance that status is inferable not literal. No report found of this line being shut, damaged, or decommissioned. Tier held at medium rather than high because the 2026 source corroborates the km-91 junction/network's liveness, not a verbatim restatement of the 'Attahaddy/km-91.5' segment name.

OPEC ASB Table 4.10 is explicitly titled 'Gas pipelines in OPEC Members'; the Attahaddy/km-91.5 line sits in the Libya gas-pipeline section. Libya Observer (2026) independently describes the same Sirte network node carrying 'gas supplies' / 'gas pumping operations'. Both sources agree fuel = gas.

OPEC ASB 2012, Table 4.10, p.75: 'Attahaddy/km-91.5', Sirte Oil, capacity 28,320,589 (1,000 scm/yr) = 28.32 bcm/yr -- an exact match to the GEM value. Searched for a second independent figure (academic papers on the Attahaddy field, e.g. the Walsh Medical Media geosciences-study abstract and a Glasgow PhD thesis abstract on Attahaddy seismic stratigraphy) but neither discusses surface pipeline infrastructure/capacity, only subsurface geology. No second source found; single strong source -> medium.

Same OPEC ASB row lists length as 25 miles = 40.23 km, matching the GEM value of 40.00 km (rounded on conversion). No independent second source with a length figure found despite the same searches as the Capacity unit.

OPEC ASB 2012 Table 4.10 gives a single diameter of 30 inches for the 'Attahaddy/km-91.5' line -- confirms the '30' half of the GEM value '30, 12' in. No source found (OPEC or otherwise) for the second '12 in' figure; it is not itemized anywhere OPEC's table shows for this segment (the adjacent 'Km-91.5/Brega' continuation is 36 in, not 12 in). Flagging: the '12 in' component of the compound Diameter value is unsupported by any source found -- may reflect a lateral/gathering spur not captured in the OPEC trunk-line table, or may warrant a second look. Value only partially corroborated, hence low tier; not marking DEAD_LINK since the ref genuinely and verifiably supports part of the stated value.

Both sources place the Attahaddy field / km-91.5 / Brega corridor entirely within Libya (Sirte Basin gas-gathering network feeding the Brega complex on the Libyan coast). StartCountryOrArea/EndCountryOrArea = Libya is trivially and doubly supported.

OPEC ASB names the direct owner/operator of this line as 'Sirte Oil'. A U.S. Department of the Treasury press release (tg1114, sanctions-related) independently lists Sirte Oil Co. among the companies owned/controlled by Libya's state-owned National Oil Corporation, establishing the chain Sirte Oil -> wholly-owned NOC operating subsidiary. This supports GEM's Owner1 = 'Libyan National Oil Corp' (100%) as a parent-company rollup of the OPEC-named direct operator, rather than either source literally naming 'Libyan National Oil Corp' as the pipeline's owner. Tier held at medium (not high) because both citable sources confirm the *relationship* rather than either directly stating NOC as owner-of-record for this specific pipeline; Wikipedia's Sirte Oil Company article says the same but was not cited as a third source to avoid tertiary-only reliance.
